# Generics: types and procedures

Writing one procedure for `int`, then copying it for `string`, then again for `float`, gets old
fast. Nim solves this with *generics*: one declaration written once, after which the compiler makes
a version for every type that is used.

The part that goes wrong is not the syntax but the constraints. Without a constraint, the compiler
accepts any type and complains deep inside. With a constraint, the wrong type is rejected at the
call site, with a reason attached.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write generic procedures and types, put constraints on a type parameter,
read the error when a constraint is not met, and tell automatic inference apart from explicit type
arguments.
:::

## One procedure for many types

Type parameters are written in square brackets after the procedure name.

```{.nim}
proc identity[T](value: T): T =
  value

echo identity(42)
echo identity("nim")
```

```{.txt}
42
nim
```

`T` is a name for a type that is not fixed yet. When `identity(42)` is called, the compiler fills
`T` with `int`; when `identity("nim")` is called, `T` becomes `string`. Filling in `T` is called
instantiation, and the result is two different procedures both named `identity`.

The name `T` lives only inside that declaration, and the two instantiated procedures share no code:
one works with `int`, the other with `string`. As a result, a mistake inside a generic body only
shows up once one of its versions is created. The compiler checks each version separately, and its
error messages often name the type being resolved.

## Type constraints: `T: SomeInteger`

Without a constraint, `T` may be any type inside the procedure body. When the body only makes sense
for some types, constrain `T` after a colon.

```{.nim}
proc double[T: SomeInteger](value: T): T =
  value * 2

echo double(21)
echo double(5'i8)
```

```{.txt}
42
10
```

`SomeInteger` is the set of integer types: signed (`int`, `int8` up to `int64`) and unsigned (`uint`
and friends). As long as `T` is in it, `value * 2` is valid. A type outside the set is rejected, and
the message explains why.

```{.nim}
proc double[T: SomeInteger](value: T): T =
  value * 2

echo double(2.5)
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(4, 12) Error: type mismatch
Expression: double(2.5)
  [1] 2.5: float64

Expected one of (first mismatch at [position]):
[1] proc double[T: SomeInteger](value: T): T
```

The last line shows the only candidate, `double` with the requirement `T: SomeInteger`. `float64` is
not part of `SomeInteger`, so no version of `double` matches. Without the constraint, a message like
this would only appear inside the body, after `T` was already used.

## Generics on types

The `[T]` brackets apply to types too, not just procedures. An `object` can take a type parameter,
so its contents adapt.

```{.nim}
type Box[T] = object
  value: T

proc boxed[T](value: T): Box[T] =
  Box[T](value: value)

echo boxed(7).value
echo boxed("text").value
```

```{.txt}
7
text
```

`Box[int]` and `Box[string]` are two different types made from one declaration. The constructor is
written `Box[T](value: value)`, and `T` there is adjusted from the value passed in.

A procedure that works on `Box[T]` must also carry the same type parameter. That is why `boxed` is
written `boxed[T]`, not just `boxed`. Without `[T]`, the compiler does not know which type is meant
inside `Box[T]`.

## Inference and explicit type arguments

The compiler infers `T` from an argument that has type `T`. When there is no such argument, `T` must
be named directly.

```{.nim}
proc makeSeq[T](count: int): seq[T] =
  for _ in 1..count:
    result.add default(T)

echo makeSeq[int](3)
echo makeSeq[string](2)
```

```{.txt}
@[0, 0, 0]
@["", ""]
```

Here `T` does not appear in the parameter list, so `makeSeq(3)` is not enough: the compiler has no
way to guess the element type. The type argument goes in square brackets after the name:
`makeSeq[int](3)`. `default(T)` produces the empty value of type `T`, which is `0` for `int` and
`""` for `string`.

## `typedesc`: taking a type as an argument

Sometimes what is passed is not a value but the type itself. A parameter of type `typedesc` accepts
that type.

```{.nim}
proc nameOf(T: typedesc): string =
  $T

echo nameOf(int)
echo nameOf(string)
```

```{.txt}
int
string
```

`nameOf(int)` does not pass a value `int`, but the type `int` itself. Calls like this are common in
the standard library, for example to create an empty collection of a given type.

## `static[T]`: a value known at compile time

A type parameter can be marked `static`. This means its value must be known at compile time, not
while the program runs.

```{.nim}
proc fill[T; N: static int](value: T): array[N, T] =
  for i in 0..<N:
    result[i] = value

echo fill[char, 3]('z')
echo fill[int, 2](9)
```

```{.txt}
['z', 'z', 'z']
[9, 9]
```

`N` is used as the size of `array[N, T]`, and an array size must be fixed, so `N` has to be known to
the compiler. Since `N` does not appear in the value parameter list, both are written explicitly:
`fill[char, 3]`. The result of `fill[char, 3]('z')` is an array of three characters. The size `N` is
part of the result type, so `fill[int, 2](9)` produces `array[2, int]`, a different type from
`fill[int, 3](9)`.

## Exercises

1. Write `proc largest[T](items: openArray[T]): T` that returns the largest value, then call it with
   an `int` array and with a `string` sequence.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   proc pair[T](value: T): (T, T) =
     (value, value)

   echo pair(3)
   echo pair("a")
   ```
3. Why can `makeSeq(3)` not be compiled without `[int]`? Explain by pointing to where `T` appears.
4. The code below fails to compile. Fix the constraint, then explain the message:
   ```{.nim}
   proc double[T: SomeInteger](value: T): T =
     value * 2

   echo double(2.5)
   ```

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- Type parameters are written `[T]` after the name; the compiler makes one version per type used.
- A constraint such as `T: SomeInteger` rejects mismatched types at the call site.
- `[T]` is also used on `type`, not only on procedures.
- `T` is inferred from arguments of type `T`; when there are none, write the type argument
  explicitly.
- `typedesc` takes a type as an argument, and `static` demands a value known at compile time.

## Next

The next chapter covers *templates*: code that the compiler copies into the call site, unlike a
generic, which creates a new version of a procedure.
